stimulus.text:
“Our very first Christmas at Hull House, when we as yet knew nothing of child labor, a number of little girls refused the candy which was offered them as part of the Christmas good cheer, saying simply that they “worked in a candy factory and could not bear the sight of it.” We discovered that for six weeks they had worked from seven in the morning until nine at night, and they were exhausted as well as satiated.”

Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X, describing Christmas 1889.
stimulus.source_note: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X. Public domain; text checked against the University of Pennsylvania digital edition.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter X

stem: According to Addams, why did the little girls refuse the candy?

options.text: They disliked the taste of candy
options.misconception: Guesses at taste when the girls name their work.

options.text: Their parents had forbidden them to eat sweets
options.misconception: Invents a parent’s rule the passage never gives.

options.text: They had already eaten too much at home
options.misconception: Guesses at a full stomach instead of factory work.

options.text: They worked in a candy factory and hated it

rationales.A: The girls say nothing about taste. They speak about their factory work.
rationales.B: No parent’s rule is mentioned. The girls explain it themselves.
rationales.C: The girls had not eaten too much at home. They were sick of candy from factory work.
rationales.D: Addams quotes the girls: they worked in a candy factory and could not bear the sight of it.
rationales.general:
Use the girls’ own words.
1. The girls refused the candy at Christmas.
2. They said they worked in a candy factory.
3. They said they could not bear the sight of it.
4. Their reason is their work, not taste or a parent’s rule.
5. A quoted reason beats any guess about why someone acted.
Remember: when a passage quotes a reason, use the quoted reason.
